newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - New products seen driving US drug firms.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - New products seen driving US drug firms.

text.p: Following a year that saw major new drugs to treat schizophrenia, AIDS, Alzheimer's disease and obesity, the U.S. drug industry is expected to extend its run of new product approvals in 1997, fueling industry profits into the next century.

The battle for market share amongst a new generation of anti-psychotic drugs will likely heat up in 1997. Meanwhile potential blockbuster treatments for diabetes, high cholesterol and balding men could hit the market.
With the new drugs typically carrying higher sales margins than older-line therapies "it should really push the drug companies' earnings ahead," Rodman & Renshaw analyst James Keeney said.

An area of fierce new competition will be in treating schizophrenia, said to affect one in 100 Americans. Analysts estimate the U.S. market for anti-psychotics at about $1 billion a year, with the potential to more than double by the end of the decade.

Johnson and Johnson describes its Risperdal, launched in the U.S. in 1994, as the most-prescribed antipsychotic in the United States. But analysts said Eli Lilly and Co's Zyprexa, which gained U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval in October, is off to a fast start in the market.

Analysts expect the next drug to join the fray will be Abbott Laboratories Inc's Serlect, which could gain FDA approval by the end of 1996. Zeneca Group Plc's Seroquel could be approved during 1997 and Pfizer Inc Ziprasidone is expected to be filed with the FDA next year.
Next year may also mark a major step forward for Warner-Lambert Co, a company in the past viewed by Wall Street more as a takeover target than as a growth company with a major drug lineup.

Warner-Lambert has two potential large selling drugs pending FDA approval: the diabetes treatment troglitazone, or Rezulin, which Warner licensed for the United States, Canada and Mexico from Japan's Sankyo Co Ltd, and the powerful cholesterol-lowering drug atorvastatin, for which it has signed up Pfizer Inc as a marketing partner.

Analysts expect Rezulin, which was recommended for approval by an FDA advisory panel last week, to be on the market in 1997's first quarter and atorvastatin to gain approval in the second half of the year. "It's a very big year for Warner," said Cowen and Co analyst Ian Sanderson.

Keeney estimates the two drugs could have combined sales of $350-to-$400 million in 1998. NatWest Securities analyst Jack Lamberton estimates Warner-Lambert in five years after they hit the market, could have Rezulin annual sales of $2 billion, with atorvastatin selling $1.2 billion a year.

In the battle against HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, Agouron Pharmaceuticals Inc is expected to file its drug Viracept with the FDA by 1997's first quarter and have it rapidly reviewed by the agency.

Viracept is a protease inhibitor drug that targets an enzyme vital to HIV's reproduction and is in the same class as drugs that gained FDA approval in 1996 market from Merck and Co Inc, Abbott Laboratories Inc. Roche Holding AG's protease inhibitor gained FDA approval in December 1995.

Agouron has said its drug could have an edge because of what it describes as a favorable combination of effectiveness, few side effects and a lower rate of the drug triggering HIV mutations that are resistant to other protease inhibitors.
The balding masses could gain hope from Merck's drug Propecia, a once-a-day pill the company says increases hair growth and prevents further hair loss in balding men.

Merck is expected to file Propecia, a lower-dose form of a Merck drug used for treating enlarged prostates, by the end of 1996, which analysts say could lead to the drug's approval in the second half of 1997.
